kept.excerpt: A new Marquette Law School Poll survey of Democratic primary voters finds Francesca Hong leading with 38%, followed by Mandela Barnes with 16%, David Crowley at 7%, and Joel Brennan and Kelda Roys at 2% each; 34% remain undecided. Including respondents who lean toward a candidate, Hong receives 46%, Barnes 21%, and Crowley 11%, with 14% undecided. The survey was conducted July 22–27, 2026, among 407 registered voters who said they would vote in the Democratic primary, including early absentee voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 6.6 percentage points. In the previous July 8–16 survey, Hong had 26% and Barnes 15%.
kept.relevance: The latest primary-source poll available at the cutoff measures Hong’s lead, its recent growth, and the substantial remaining uncertainty.

kept.excerpt: A State Navigate poll released Tuesday found Hong at 44%, Crowley at 15%, Barnes at 14%, and Roys, Brennan and Sara Rodriguez at 4% each, with 13% undecided. The survey interviewed nearly 1,100 Wisconsinites July 23–26, after Rodriguez’s withdrawal and Crowley’s reentry, and reported a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. The poll was sponsored by liberal groups UpNorthNews and Main Street Action.
kept.relevance: A separate contemporary survey corroborates Hong’s polling lead while identifying sponsorship and field dates needed to assess its evidentiary weight.

kept.excerpt: Crowley reentered the governor’s race on July 18 with an endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers, who had previously declined to support a primary candidate. Rodriguez had ended her campaign the previous day amid financial turmoil. Barnes criticized Crowley’s return, while Brennan and Roys indicated they would continue competing.
kept.relevance: The field reshuffle and Evers endorsement establish both the possibility of consolidation against Hong and the continued fragmentation among her opponents.

kept.excerpt: Hong reported raising nearly $709,000 and spending around $433,000 during the first six months of 2026, ending June with around $411,000. Barnes raised around $840,000, spent just over $1.1 million, and ended June with about $204,000. Brennan ended the period with close to $360,000, and Roys had about $406,000.
kept.relevance: The last verified fundraising report included here compares the candidates’ financial resources before the final primary stretch.

kept.excerpt: Barnes, Brennan, Crowley, Hong and Roys participated in a televised debate on July 28, largely agreeing on raising taxes on millionaires and increasing public education funding. Crowley was the only candidate to say he would have signed the failed bipartisan budget-surplus compromise. The Democratic primary was scheduled for August 11, and more than 107,000 absentee ballots had already been returned as of Tuesday, according to Wisconsin Elections Commission data.
kept.relevance: The debate report verifies the active field and election schedule immediately before the cutoff and documents voting already underway.

kept.excerpt: A Wisconsin judge ruled July 29 that voters who had already returned absentee ballots for the primary could not void them and request new ballots. More than 117,000 absentee ballots had been returned by Wednesday. Rodriguez’s name remained on the ballot, along with Missy Hughes, who had dropped out in June.
kept.relevance: The ruling and returned-ballot count identify constraints on how candidate withdrawals and late campaign changes could translate into votes.

kept.excerpt: A $2.2 million television advertising campaign by the Republican Governors Association began airing July 16, describing Hong as too liberal for Wisconsin and highlighting her immigration positions. Several Democrats, including Hong’s rivals, argued that the ads were intended to increase her appeal among Democratic primary voters. Hong publicly thanked the association for highlighting her legislative proposals.
kept.relevance: The report documents significant outside spending focused on Hong and the competing contemporary interpretations of its primary-election effects.
